1.title: Diagnosing and Fixing Poor Outputs
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Diagnosing and Fixing Poor Outputs. This module covers diagnosing and fixing poor outputs. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. A method to diagnose a weak output: observe, isolate, change one thing, test. A symptom to cause to fix table for the most common problems. How to troubleshoot features, files and errors. How to use feedback to adjust your approach.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Disappointing Replies
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Disappointing Replies. Care agents complain that Claude's reply drafts are too long, too stiff and sometimes quote the wrong policy. The team lead does not rewrite everything. They collect five bad examples, find the pattern and change one thing at a time.

1.title: A Diagnostic Method
1.text: A Diagnostic Method. The figure shows this: Diagnose in a loop: observe the symptom, find the pattern, guess the cause, change one thing, test and record. Observe: what exactly is wrong? Save the prompt and the bad output. Find the pattern: is it every time, or only for some inputs? Compare good and bad cases. Hypothesize the cause: missing context, unclear instruction, conflicting rules, wrong feature, stale knowledge, wrong model, or a limit.

1.title: A Diagnostic Method, continued
1.text: A Diagnostic Method, continued. Change one thing: a clearer instruction, an example, a source file, a different feature or model. Test on the same inputs and compare. Keep what works; log it. Changing many things at once hides which change helped. Test on several cases, including awkward ones, not only the one that failed. Exam tip: The expected approach is systematic and minimal: diagnose the cause, change one variable, retest. Starting over completely, or switching to the biggest model first, is usually not the best answer.

1.title: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes
1.text: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes. Generic or vague answer. Likely cause: Missing goal, audience, context. Fix: Add purpose, audience, facts, an example (Module one). Wrong format or length. Likely cause: Format not specified. Fix: State structure, word count, fields; give an example. Ignores a rule. Likely cause: Rule buried, vague, conflicting, or too many rules. Fix: Put it clearly and early; explain why; remove conflicts; shorten the list. Invented facts or sources. Likely cause: No source provided; Claude fills gaps. Fix: Provide the source; ask to quote it; allow "not covered"; verify (Modules three and four). Outdated information. Likely cause: Knowledge cutoff. Fix: Use web search; check dates.

1.title: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued
1.text: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued. Forgets earlier instructions; repeats itself. Likely cause: Long, drifted context. Fix: Summarize and restart; move standing rules into a Project (Modules eight and eleven). Inconsistent tone across outputs. Likely cause: No voice reference. Fix: Add examples, a style or Project instructions. Shallow reasoning on a hard task. Likely cause: Task too big for one step, or light model or low effort. Fix: Break into steps; use thinking; try a stronger model or higher effort. Misreads a document. Likely cause: Poor file type, scanned pages, large file. Fix: Check file type and limits; split; ask for quotes; try text version.

1.title: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued
1.text: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued. Spreadsheet or script fails. Likely cause: Untested output, wrong tool version. Fix: Test on a sample; give the exact error message back to Claude; state your tool and version. Claims it did something it could not (sent an email, saved a file). Likely cause: No integration exists. Fix: Check the destination; enable the connector or do the step yourself. Links do not work. Likely cause: Produced from memory. Fix: Open every link; ask for sources and verify. Refuses a legitimate request. Likely cause: Wording looks like a prohibited request, or context is missing. Fix: Explain the legitimate purpose and context; rephrase; if truly restricted, follow policy.

1.title: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued
1.text: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued. Biased or one-sided. Likely cause: Leading prompt or skewed data. Fix: Ask for balance; neutral wording; check data (Module three). Too slow or limit reached. Likely cause: Heavy tools, high effort, long chat. Fix: Lower effort, lighter model, new chat (Module sixteen).

1.title: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued
1.text: Symptoms, Causes and Fixes, continued. The figure shows this: A symptom-to-fix chooser: vague answers need context, ignored rules need clearer instructions, invented facts need sources, forgotten context needs a restart or a Project, shallow reasoning needs steps or a stronger setting.

1.title: Feature, File and Error Problems
1.text: Feature, File and Error Problems. Web search not used. Is it available and on? Say "search the web"; on Team and Enterprise the owner must enable it. Research seems inactive. Prompt directly: "please use the research tool"; web search must be on; on mobile connectors are skipped. Skill not applied. Skills need code execution on; toggle the skill on; the description must say when to use it; be explicit in the request. Skills section greyed out. Code execution (Create and edit files) is off for you or your organization. Spreadsheet (X L S X) upload fails. X L S X needs code execution and file creation turned on.

1.title: Feature, File and Error Problems, continued
1.text: Feature, File and Error Problems, continued. File too large or too long. Chat limits: five hundred megabytes per file, twenty files, P D F s up to one thousand pages; split documents. Connector not pulling data. Reconnect from Customize greater than Connectors; confirm you have access; use web or Desktop (not mobile) for Research with connectors. "Message will exceed the length limit". Attach fewer or smaller files, split or summarize, or start a new chat. "Approaching" or "reached" usage limit. Wait for the five-hour or weekly reset, reduce usage, or use credits if enabled. "Due to unexpected capacity constraints". System-wide demand, not your fault; wait a few minutes and retry.

1.title: Feature, File and Error Problems, continued
1.text: Feature, File and Error Problems, continued. Login error. Turn off V P N and extensions, clear cache and cookies, check the status page. Output blocked by content filtering. Rephrase the request; check it is within the Usage Policy.

1.title: Using Feedback and Results
1.text: Using Feedback and Results. Collect feedback from users: what failed, how often, in what situation. Use real examples, not impressions. Thumbs-down a bad response to report it; it helps improve the product but does not fix your prompt. Adjust the layer where the cause lies: prompt (wording), Project (instructions, knowledge), skill (method), model or effort, feature (search, Research, files), or process (add a review step). Measure before and after: error rate, time to finish, satisfaction (Module sixteen). Share what you learn: update the prompt library and instructions so others benefit.

1.title: Using Feedback and Results, continued
1.text: Using Feedback and Results, continued. Know when to stop or escalate: if the same task fails after clear prompts, correct knowledge and a stronger model, the task may be a poor fit, or it may need a Developer's help (Module ten). Exam tip: Change one thing at a time and retest: changing everything at once hides what worked. Exam tip: If Claude says it did something (sent, saved, booked), check the destination before you trust it.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Method: Observe, pattern, cause, change one thing, test, record. Generic output: Add context, audience, example. Ignored rule: Clearer, earlier, with a reason; fewer rules. Invented facts: Provide the source; quote; allow "not covered"; verify. Forgetful: Summarize and restart; Project for standing rules. Tone drift: Examples, style, Project instructions. Shallow reasoning: Steps, thinking, stronger model or effort. Claimed actions: Check the destination; enable the connector or do it yourself. Feature fails: Check the toggle, plan, code execution, limits, description. Feedback: Use real examples; adjust the right layer; measure; share lessons.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A team's reply drafts keep running too long. What is the best first change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Format and length problems usually come from an unspecified format; fix the prompt first.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Claude keeps quoting the wrong return window. The Project contains two policy versions. What should the owner do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Conflicting knowledge is a likely cause; fix the source and test.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An analyst changes the model, the prompt, the files and the settings all at once, and the output improves. What is the weakness of this approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Change one variable at a time to learn what works.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Claude says it emailed a supplier, but no email integration is connected. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Claude can overstate its abilities; check the destination.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A custom skill is installed but Claude never uses it. What should you check first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A skill that is off, a disabled code execution setting or a vague description are the documented reasons Claude does not use it.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two are good responses to a long chat that has started to contradict itself? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Restart with a summary and persist the rules properly.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A spreadsheet formula from Claude returns an error in Google Sheets. What is the best next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Give Claude the evidence and test the fix on a small sample.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: C. Question four: B. Question five: B. Question six: A and B. Question seven: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
